desc:
You are given a string s and a list of operations. Each operation is a pair [dir, k]:

  • dir = 0: rotate left by k, i.e. move the first k characters to the end (in order);
  • dir = 1: rotate right by k, i.e. move the last k characters to the front (in order).

The operations are applied one after another. Return the final string. Note that k may be larger than the length of the string.

s = "abcdef", ops = [[0, 2], [1, 5], [0, 1]]
result = "efabcd"

The string goes abcdef → cdefab → defabc → efabcd.
hints: Performing every rotation on the string costs O(n) each. Think about what the net result of a long sequence of rotations is.
A rotation to the right by k is the same as a rotation to the left by -k, and rotating by the length n changes nothing. Rotations of a cycle just add up.
Keep a single offset: add k for a left rotation, subtract k for a right rotation. At the end, reduce the offset modulo n and cut the string once: s[off:] + s[:off].
editorial: All the operations are rotations of the same cyclic sequence, so they compose by adding their shifts. Let the offset be the total number of positions the string was rotated to the left: a left rotation by k adds k, a right rotation subtracts k. Only the offset modulo n matters, because n single steps return to the start.

After processing all operations, the answer is the string rotated left by off mod n, built with one slice concatenation. Total time is O(n + m) for n characters and m operations, with O(n) space for the result.
solution:
def applyRotations(s, ops):
    n = len(s)
    off = 0
    for d, k in ops:
        off += k if d == 0 else -k
    off %= n
    return s[off:] + s[:off]
